Building a Spark-Fill Surface

A step-by-step walkthrough of the whole pipeline from one random walk to a rendered map — surface.py's spark-fill construction, then palette.py/postprocess.py/render.py's route to a coloured image — each step with its own figure.

1

Overview

Spark-fill builds a heightfield in two stages: lay down a connected seed path, then fill every other cell by repeated neighbour-averaging. Run n_walks independent copies of that and combine them by taking the highest value at each cell, and that's the whole generator — Steps 1-4 below. Steps 5-8 continue on into the rest of the real pipeline (cli.generate_map): quantize the result into palette bins, patch single-cell artifacts, trace elevation contours, and render — the same one surface, generated once and carried through every step, so Fig. 8's finished map is traceable all the way back to Fig. 1's single walk. The grid wraps at every edge (a torus), so it tiles seamlessly and a walk or a fill region can cross an edge and continue on the opposite side.

Two implementation notes that apply throughout: values live in [-1, 1] and are clamped there at every write, and every source of randomness comes from Python's own random module, called sequentially — nothing here is vectorized or batched, which is part of why the fill order (Step 2) needs its own care.

2

Step 1 — The seed path

generate_brownian_spark_surface starts from one uniformly random cell, then takes sparks steps of a random walk: at each step, move one cell down or one cell right, chosen with equal probability, wrapping at the grid's edges. Every visited cell — the start plus all sparks steps — is recorded as a seed and will be set to seed_value (deep sea, -1.0 by default) once filling begins.

Only moving down or right (never up or left) means the path can't double back on itself, so it stays a single connected curve rather than a tangle — that's what "connected seed path" buys over just scattering sparks independent random points (generate_spark_surface, the older, simpler sibling of this function): a curve of seeds produces one contiguous basin once filled, where independent scattered points each grow their own separate little region and only merge where two fill fronts happen to meet.

3

Step 2 — Filling by neighbour-averaging

Everything that isn't a seed starts empty. _fill_from_seeds repeats the following until nothing is empty: collect every still-empty cell, shuffle that list into a random order, then go through it in that order and, for each cell, look at its four grid neighbours (up, down, left, right, wrapping at the edges). If at least one of those neighbours already has a value, set this cell to the average of the known neighbours plus a small random jitter (random.uniform(-step, step)), clamped back into [-1, 1]. If none of its neighbours are filled yet, leave it empty for the next pass.

Two details worth being explicit about, both directly visible above:

  • The shuffle isn't cosmetic. Without it, filling in a fixed order (say, row by row) leaves a visible directional grain — every cell would systematically look toward the same side for its "known" neighbours. Shuffling the pending list each pass means the fill front advances roughly evenly in every direction instead, which is what keeps Fig. 2's frontier looking like a growing blob rather than a sweeping wave.
  • A pass isn't atomic. Cells are written one at a time within a shuffled pass, in place — so a cell filled earlier in the same pass can already supply a "known" neighbour value to a cell reached later in that same pass, rather than every cell only ever seeing the previous pass's values. This is part of why the fill can finish in far fewer passes than the grid's diameter would otherwise require.
4

Step 3 — One walk, complete

Once nothing is left empty, one call to generate_brownian_spark_surface is done. The result is a single heightfield: one basin, its shape set by the seed path's route and by whatever the accumulated jitter happened to do along the way.

5

Step 4 — Combining multiple walks

generate_multi_spark_surface runs Steps 1-3 independently n_walks times — each with its own fresh random seed path, sharing nothing with the others — and combines the resulting heightfields cell-wise by taking the maximum at every cell, not the average.

Max rather than average matters specifically because of what each walk's seed_value represents: averaging three fields together would pull every cell back toward that shared low value wherever the three walks disagree, flattening exactly the high points a max preserves. Whether three walks end up producing three visually distinct islands or one broader landmass depends on how close together their random start points and routes happen to land — nothing in the algorithm forces separation, it only refuses to erase a peak once one walk has produced it.

6

Step 5 — Quantizing into palette bins

palette.normalize_surface maps every continuous value in [-1, 1] to an integer palette index. The split is asymmetric, matching the palette's own asymmetry: values <= 0 ("sea") map into the bottom low_bins indices, values > 0 ("land") map into the remaining n_bins - 2 indices on top. Each side is truncated (not rounded) into place — int(value * scale) — so this is a genuine quantization, not a smoothing: two nearby values that happen to straddle a bin edge end up in different bins with nothing in between.

7

Step 6 — Cleaning isolated points

postprocess.clean_isolated_points checks every cell against its four (wrapping) neighbours; if a cell's value matches none of them, it's replaced by whichever value is most common among those four. The intent is to patch single-cell speckle — a lone pixel that ended up in the wrong bin purely from the fill's per-cell jitter (Step 2).

8

Step 7 — Tracing elevation contours

postprocess.compute_isocurves calls skimage.measure.find_contours once per level, 0 through n_levels - 1, each call tracing every place the cleaned, quantized field crosses that level as a closed or edge-terminating line. The result is a separate list of contour lines per level — n_levels independent line sets, not one combined drawing.

9

Step 8 — Rendering

render.render_surface does the final assembly: matplotlib.imshow paints the quantized, cleaned index array through ListedColormap(rgb_palette) — each integer index becomes one fixed colour from the loaded palette, no interpolation between bins — then every level's contour lines from Step 7 are drawn on top, each in its own palette colour.
